idiom_name: one unit owning both directions (two functions or methods, or a registry keyed by the (source, target) pair)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: put both directions of a representation pair in one unit - a class with two methods (to_target/from_source, encode/decode, convert_from/convert_to) or a pair of free functions colocated in the pair's own module - and let a registry or factory resolve it from the (source, target) pair, so callers never import the other representation. Keep converters stateless and pure: no I/O and no lazy access across the boundary. Provide an element-wise path for collections and streams so batch mapping is not re-implemented per call site, decide the failure mode once (raise, result type, option, default) and document it, and keep the two directions exact inverses where the data allows it - where it does not, name the normalization explicitly. The classic class structure is justified only when several callers, formats or configurations share one converter; a private pair of functions in the same module is otherwise the better shape. For lawful bidirectional converters (isomorphisms), both round-trip laws must hold: forward -> backward -> forward == id and backward -> forward -> backward == id (see lawful-conversions Haskell library, Higher-Kinded-J Iso).
code_sketch:
converter.to_wire(domain)      -> payload
converter.from_wire(payload)   -> domain
converter.map_all(domains)     -> payloads     # element-wise, no loop at call sites

# registry.register((Domain, Payload), converter)
# both directions live in one unit; Domain and Payload import neither
# each other nor the registry
pitfalls: Implementing one direction only and letting callers invent the reverse, so the reverse silently diverges from the mapping rules.
A converter that is not the exact inverse of its other direction, so a round trip loses or invents data.
Putting I/O or lazy loading into the mapping step: a converter that fetches data cannot be reasoned about or tested in isolation.
Leaving the mapping implicit (reflection or annotations) without a strict policy for unknown and missing fields.

Reflection-based mapper performance trap: ModelMapper and similar runtime-convention mappers allocate ~12 KB per mapping and run ~300x slower than hand-written or compile-time-generated code; never use them in hot paths without benchmarking.

Silent type erasure bugs: tools that copy fields by name without verifying type compatibility (BeanUtils, some convention-based mappers) can silently coerce incompatible types, producing objects that compile but fail at runtime with ClassCastException.
Stale library risk: Orika (unmaintained since 2019) and Dozer have known compatibility issues with modern Java; choosing them for a new project accrues technical debt from the start.

Implicit lossy round-trips: a converter that injects defaults on the forward direction and silently drops fields on the reverse produces round-trip values that differ from the original without any error or warning; round-trip property tests are the only reliable guard.

Unidirectional drift: when only the write direction (domain -> DTO) is implemented and the read direction is reconstructed ad hoc by callers, any domain field added to the read path is silently omitted until a production incident exposes it.

Mutable collection types without ValueComparer (EF Core): mapping a List<T> through a ValueConverter without a ValueComparer causes reference-equality tracking bugs; the comparer must implement sequence-equality for correct change detection.

Violating round-trip laws for lawful isomorphisms: a converter claiming to be an isomorphism that is not (e.g., a normalizing converter that canonicalizes strings) silently violates the round-trip law; mark such converters explicitly as non-invertible or canonicalizing and avoid using them where isomorphism is assumed.

Null propagation asymmetry: one direction accepts null (returns null) while the reverse rejects it with an exception; this inconsistency causes NPEs in callers that do not know which direction they are using; decide and document null semantics symmetrically.

Wrong move: relying on convention-based auto-mappers (AutoMapper, ModelMapper) at domain boundaries -> renamed or retyped properties silently drop out of the mapping at runtime with no compile-time signal, and complex profiles erase traceability -> instead keep explicit converters or compile-time code generation (MapStruct, source generators) and reserve auto-mappers for trivial 1:1 DTO copies.

Wrong move: implementing only sql.Scanner on a Go custom type -> parameter binding silently falls back to DefaultParameterConverter, unsupported types fail as query-time errors, and the write direction drifts from the read direction -> instead implement both Scanner and driver.Valuer on the same type so both directions share one owner.

Wrong move: overriding only Rails ActiveModel::Type::Value#cast_value -> in-memory casting looks correct while what is actually written to and re-read from the database stays uncontrolled -> instead override serialize and deserialize for the database boundary, keep cast_value for user-input coercion, and test the serialize/deserialize round trip.
